title: Nonogram Puzzle Checker
plainSentence: A nonogram maker that lets you draw a picture, get its number clues, and check whether anyone can solve it without guessing.
pitch: Draw a picture on a small grid and the page writes the number clues around it, like a picture-by-numbers puzzle. It then solves the puzzle the way a person would, one row or column at a time, and reports whether the clues have exactly one answer and whether the whole grid falls out without guessing. If it does not, it shades the stuck squares and suggests a one-square change that repairs it; then you print the puzzle sheet and an answer page.
firstMinute: A 10 by 10 sample picture is already drawn with its clues written around it, and a slow replay is solving it pass by pass in colour. A verdict card reads something like 'One answer, no guessing needed, 6 passes, easy'. Click a single square to flip it and watch the verdict change, perhaps to 'Two answers' with the ambiguous squares shaded.
conceptsToLearn: A nonogram is a picture-by-numbers grid: each number says how long a run of filled squares is in that row or column.
whyNow: Timeless: anyone who makes puzzles for a book, a class or a friend hits the same trap, a puzzle that has one answer on paper but forces guessing. The page makes that visible in seconds.

purposeDetail.job: Turn a drawn picture into nonogram clues and prove, with visible working, whether the puzzle has exactly one answer and can be finished by row-and-column logic alone.
purposeDetail.audience: Puzzle makers, teachers, parents and hobbyists who want to design nonograms that are fair to solve, and solvers curious why a puzzle got stuck.

paywallEvidence.product: A paid no-guess nonogram toolkit sold through a small-seller storefront
paywallEvidence.whatIsGated: The check that every accepted puzzle can be finished by row-and-column logic alone, plus the print-ready puzzle-book PDF with answer pages; listed at 29 US dollars as of 2026-10-13, per the seller's own listing.

purposeDetail.freeGap: Free editors exist that check solvability or uniqueness (search results mention an in-game checker on a fan wiki and an open-source editor still in development), so uniqueness alone is not the gap. Not confirmed that any free one tests the stricter no-guess property, shows each solving pass, and proposes a one-square repair. The real remaining gap is: private, in the browser, shows its working, suggests the fix. Unverified for any named free tool; the page will not compare itself to any product.
purposeDetail.oracle: Published counts of small square nonograms: the number of n by n grids whose clues give a unique solution that row-and-column logic alone can finish, from OEIS entry A391619 (1, 2, 14, 384, 51234, 24976511 for sizes 0 to 5); the broader unique-solution counts are in OEIS A242876. The built-in self-test enumerates every grid up to 4 by 4 and compares.
purposeDetail.inputs: A picture drawn by clicking or dragging on a grid from 5 by 5 to 15 by 15 (20 by 20 under More), or pasted clue numbers; a sample picture is preloaded.
purposeDetail.outputs: Clue numbers, a verdict (no solution, several solutions, one solution needing guesses, or one solution reached by logic alone), a difficulty label from the pass count, the stuck squares, a suggested one-square repair, and exports: puzzle sheet and answer page as PNG, SVG and a print layout, plus a share link holding the grid.
purposeDetail.limits: Black-and-white nonograms only, up to 20 by 20. Exhaustive checking of larger grids is capped and reported as 'could not decide' rather than guessed. Difficulty is a rough label from solving passes, not a verdict on how hard a person will find it. No photo import.

research.summary: Uniqueness and no-guess solvability are different properties. A seller of a paid toolkit says most nonogram generators check nothing or only uniqueness, while its own accepted puzzles must be finished by working one row or column at a time. The count of 5 by 5 grids that are unique and line-solvable (24,976,511 of 33,554,432) is documented, and a gap of hundreds of thousands of grids are unique but need guessing. Uniqueness checking is NP-hard in general, but a line solver is cheap and a cap on the exhaustive search keeps the page fast. That makes a faithful, auditable, in-browser checker with a repair suggestion realistic in one morning.

sources.title: No-Guess Nonogram Toolkit (seller listing)
sources.snippet: Seller listing at 29 US dollars. Says puzzles are accepted only if row-by-row and column-by-column logic finishes the grid, and that most generators check nothing or only uniqueness. Outputs a print-ready PDF with answer pages.
sources.note: The seller's own page for what it sells: price, what is gated, and the no-guess definition. Seller claims only; no independent reviews seen.

sources.title: Pixelogic Weekly issue 14
sources.snippet: Defines logically solvable as unique solution plus line-solvable, gives a small 5 by 5 puzzle with one answer where row-by-row work gets stuck, and quotes a brute-force count of 24,976,511 for 5 by 5.
sources.note: Documents that unique does not imply line-solvable, and the 5 by 5 count.

sources.title: Hacker News thread about a 5 by 5 nonogram game (mirror)
sources.snippet: Discussion where 24,976,511 is given as the number of 5 by 5 grids solvable by logic, and a commenter points to a larger count of uniquely solvable grids from OEIS.
sources.note: Second independent mention of the 5 by 5 count; the larger unique-solution count is a commenter's claim here.

sources.title: OEIS A391619
sources.snippet: Sequence for n by n nonograms solvable by analysing each row and column in isolation without guessing; per the search summary its data begins 1, 2, 14, 384, 51234, 24976511.
sources.note: Named oracle for the self-test. The data line was reported in a search summary, not read on the page itself; it agrees with the 24,976,511 figure from two other sites.

sources.title: OEIS A242876
sources.snippet: Counts n by n nonograms (hanjie) that can be solved uniquely; about 75 percent of 5 by 5 grids; cites Ueda and Nagao for hardness of uniqueness.
sources.note: Broader unique-solution count. The exact 5 by 5 value 25,309,575 was relayed by a forum commenter, not seen in this entry's data line, so that number stays unverified.

sources.title: On Solving Simple Curved Nonograms (arXiv 2505.01554)
sources.snippet: Background on nonogram complexity: existence is NP-complete, uniqueness of a given solution is NP-hard, and 'simple' nonograms are those a polynomial method solves cell by cell.
sources.note: Supports why an exhaustive uniqueness check needs a cap while the line solver is cheap, and that simple versus non-simple puzzles exist.

sources.title: Nonograms Katana wiki: My Nonograms
sources.snippet: Describes a built-in checker that tries to solve a submitted puzzle and rejects ones with several solutions or only trivial lines.
sources.note: Example of a free in-game uniqueness checker, for freeGap. Single result.

sources.title: number loom (itch.io page)
sources.snippet: Open-source HTML5 nonogram editor listed as in development that tracks solvability as you edit; MIT-licensed code.
sources.note: Example of a free editor with solvability tracking, for freeGap. Single result; not opened.

sources.title: Solvability of nonograms (Patrick Stevens)
sources.snippet: Blog post asking whether every nonogram is solvable and uniquely so; result snippet did not show its conclusions.
sources.note: Background only; no claim rests on it.

facts.claim: As of 2026-10-13, a seller's own listing offers a no-guess nonogram toolkit for 29 US dollars. It accepts a puzzle only if working one row or column at a time, filling only forced squares, finishes the grid, and it says most generators check nothing or only uniqueness.
A nonogram can have exactly one solution and still not be solvable by row-and-column logic alone; such puzzles are outside the class of line-solvable ('simple') nonograms.
Of the 33,554,432 possible 5 by 5 grids, 24,976,511 give puzzles that are unique and solvable by line logic alone; per OEIS A391619 the series for sizes 0 to 5 begins 1, 2, 14, 384, 51234, 24976511.
Deciding whether a given nonogram solution is the only one is NP-hard, so an exhaustive uniqueness check on large grids needs a work cap.
Free tools with some solvability or uniqueness check exist (a fan-wiki in-game checker and an open-source editor in development), so uniqueness alone is not the gap.

inspirations: level editors with a built-in playtest

design.coreLoop: Input, output, refine: draw or edit squares, see clues and the verdict update instantly, replay the solver pass by pass, apply the suggested repair or redraw, then export when the verdict is green.
sophisticationHooks: Pass-coloured replay: each square is tinted by the pass in which logic fixed it, so the rating is visible, not just a number
Stuck squares shaded when logic stops, plus an exhaustive count of answers up to two with a node cap and an honest 'could not decide'
One-square repair search: try flipping each square and report flips that make the puzzle unique and line-solvable
Self-test panel that enumerates every grid up to 4 by 4 and checks the counts against published sequences
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: drawing grid (5, 10, 15; 20 under More), clue generator, line solver with pass replay, depth-first answer counter with cap, difficulty label, single-flip repair, PNG/SVG/print export, share link in the page address, self-test. Cut: coloured nonograms, photo import, puzzle packs, uploads, accounts.
risks: The paywall claim rests on one seller listing (its own page, so verified under the primary-source rule, but no independent reviews); the page will not name or compare with any product.
The exact 5 by 5 unique-solution count 25,309,575 is unverified; the self-test uses only the line-solvable series, and shows any other number as 'as of 2026-10-13, per OEIS' or leaves it out.
The OEIS data line for A391619 came through a search summary; a verifier should re-open it before the sequence is printed on the page.
Brute-force on all 33 million 5 by 5 grids may be slow in a browser; mitigate by making the 4 by 4 check automatic and the 5 by 5 check an optional worker run with a progress bar.
A drawn grid has many focusable squares; it must be one composite widget with a single tab stop and arrow-key movement so the first screen stays within 8 controls.
Difficulty by pass count is a rough proxy; the page says so rather than claiming a human rating.
The lens brief's claim that the best forge teaches itself first is a design opinion, not a fact; the page carries a short worked 'why guessing happens' example instead.
